study_identification_part.si4_title: Individualized functional connectome abnormalities obtained using two normative model unveil neurophysiological subtypes of obsessive compulsive disorder

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To identify neurophysiological subtypes of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) based on individualized functional connectome abnormalities obtained using normative models of functional connectivity strength (FCS), addressing the high heterogeneity observed among OCD patients.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: K-means clustering (k=2 to 10, 100 iterations per k) using individualized FCS abnormalities (Z-score vectors, 246×1 per patient) as features, with silhouette values to determine optimal number of subtypes; Two-sample t-tests comparing each subtype vs. HCs, controlling for age, sex, and mean FD, with Bonferroni correction (p<0.05); Group comparisons of demographic and clinical variables between subtypes (age, sex, educational level, Y-BOCS, illness duration, age of onset) using chi-square tests and two-sample t-tests; Comparison of mean FD between subtypes to assess motion effects; Reproducibility analyses: (1) 1000 iterations of subsampling 90% of patients with calculation of Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between subsample and full sample clustering; (2) Validation using AAL atlas (90 and 116 regions) with ARI calculation between atlases
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Two OCD subtypes were identified with opposite FCS patterns: subtype 1 (73.74%) showed decreased FCS in frontal, insular, hippocampal and sensorimotor regions, while subtype 2 (26.26%) showed increased FCS in widespread brain regions; subtypes differed significantly in age of onset (p=0.014), with subtype 1 having later onset.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using normative modeling of functional connectivity strength (FCS) and k-means clustering, the study identified two distinct OCD subtypes with opposite deviation patterns. Subtype 1 (73.74%, n=73) exhibited significantly decreased FCS (Bonferroni-corrected p<0.05) primarily in the superior medial frontal gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, temporal gyrus, insula, parahippocampal gyrus, hippocampus, precentral/postcentral gyrus, and middle occipital gyrus. Subtype 2 (26.26%, n=26) demonstrated significantly increased FCS (Bonferroni-corrected p<0.05) in distributed regions including the superior medial frontal gyrus, inferior frontal gyrus, middle frontal gyrus, thalamus, striatum, and middle occipital gyrus. When all OCD patients were analyzed together, no significant FCS abnormalities were detected relative to healthy controls. The two subtypes showed significant differences in age (subtype 1: slightly older, t=2.17, p=0.032) and age of onset (subtype 1: mean 18.28±10.53 years; subtype 2: mean 11.49±7.14 years; t=2.52, p=0.014), but did not differ in sex, educational level, illness duration, symptom severity (Y-BOCS), or head motion (mean FD). Reproducibility analyses confirmed robust clustering: the average Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) between subsamples and the full cohort was 0.91±0.08; validation using the AAL atlas also identified two subtypes with similar contrasting FCS patterns (ARI=0.43 between parcellation schemes). Individual-level heterogeneity was substantial: 44.44% of OCD patients showed extreme negative deviations (|Z|>1.96) in at least one region, while 21.21% showed extreme positive deviations, but overlap across patients in any single region was very low.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Cross-sectional design limits assessment of subtype stability and generalizability; No independent external validation dataset; Limited clinical information restricted exploration of clinical differences between subtypes; Body mass index and alcohol/cigarette use not controlled; OCD patients had lower educational levels than HCs (though this did not differ between subtypes)
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Firstly, our study was conducted using a cross-sectional sample, which raises questions about the stability and generalizability of the identified subtypes. Validation of our results should be pursued using an independent dataset to confirm the robustness of our findings. Secondly, the clinical information available for patients was limited, which restricted our ability to explore potential differences in other clinical aspects between the identified subtypes... Thirdly, factors such as body mass index and alcohol/cigarette use were not adequately controlled for... Lastly, patients with OCD in our study had lower educational levels compared to HCs.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study intentionally did not regress out global signal during preprocessing based on evidence that global signal variance and topography are altered in mental disorders. Correlations below r=0.2 were excluded from FCS calculation to reduce noise. The study used both the Fan et al. 2016 parcellation (246 regions) and AAL atlas (90 and 116 regions including/excluding cerebellum) for validation. Subtype differences reconcile inconsistent findings in previous OCD neuroimaging studies, suggesting that varying proportions of these subtypes across samples may explain contradictory results in the literature.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This is a single-center study from China (First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University) with first-episode, untreated OCD patients. All participants were Han Chinese and right-handed. The study builds on prior work by the same group on heterogeneity in psychiatric disorders using normative models. The normative model achieved good performance (mean standardized MSE ≈1.00) in 10-fold cross-validation on healthy controls. The identified subtypes align with clinical knowledge about early-onset vs. late-onset OCD having different genetic contributions, treatment responses, and brain connectivity patterns. The Fan et al. 2016 parcellation used is the Brainnetome atlas with 246 cortical and subcortical regions. Note: There is a discrepancy in the text stating 'ninety-eight' patients were recruited but all tables and results use N=99; this may be a typographical error. Also, Table 2 appears to have an error in the age data for subtypes (shows identical values to overall OCD and HC from Table 1), though the text correctly reports a significant age difference between subtypes.
